questions.question: What is the difference between raise, re-raising, and raise from in Python?
questions.title: raise, Re-raising, and Exception Chaining
questions.direct_answer: `raise Error(...)` starts a failure, bare `raise` preserves the active failure, and `raise NewError(...) from cause` translates it while recording the cause.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether raising, propagation, and abstraction-safe translation are distinguished.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Wrapping every exception without adding meaning, or using `raise error` for a simple re-raise.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Preserve the cause when translating a low-level failure into a stable application error.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `raise SomeError(...)` creates or raises a chosen exception.
Bare `raise` inside a handler re-raises the currently handled exception.
`raise NewError(...) from error` records an explicit causal chain.
Use translation when a lower-level type should not leak across an abstraction boundary.
Prefer bare `raise` to `raise error` when simply propagating the same failure.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The `raise` statement has three common jobs. Raising an exception instance, such as `raise ValueError("port must be positive")`, starts a failure at the point where a contract is violated. A bare `raise` inside an `except` suite sends the currently handled exception onward and preserves the original traceback. Raising a new exception `from` the caught one translates the failure while setting an explicit cause, so the traceback explains both the higher-level meaning and the lower-level reason.

For example, a configuration loader may catch the `ValueError` produced by `int(text)` and raise `ConfigurationError("invalid port") from error`. Callers now depend on the configuration abstraction rather than a parsing detail, while debugging still reveals the original conversion failure. If the loader only logs and cannot recover, bare `raise` is the simpler choice.

Writing `raise error` is legal, but it raises from that line and changes the visible traceback position; bare `raise` is preferred when the goal is to continue the same exception. `raise NewError(...) from None` suppresses display of the automatic context and can make a deliberately simplified user-facing traceback, but it should not be used merely to hide useful evidence.

The choice follows the boundary: start an error for a broken contract, re-raise when this layer cannot finish handling it, and chain a new type when translating to a clearer abstraction.

sections.title: Translation should preserve both meanings
sections.content:
When an exception is raised while another is being handled, Python records the earlier one as context. Explicit `from` states that the earlier exception is the direct cause. Debugging tools can then show a two-level story: what the low-level operation reported and what that means to the current service.

Translation is useful at stable interfaces. A repository might turn a driver-specific error into `StorageUnavailableError`; business code should not need to import the database driver's types. Translation becomes harmful when every function wraps every error with a vague new message, producing a long chain without adding meaning.

Bare re-raising belongs in a handler that records context or performs partial cleanup but cannot declare success. The active exception is available only while a handler is running, so bare `raise` outside that situation produces a runtime error.

sections.title: Choose the form by intent
sections.content:
| Intent | Form | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Report a violated rule | `raise ValueError("...")` | Starts that exception |
| Continue the same failure | `raise` | Preserves the active exception and traceback |
| Translate an abstraction | `raise AppError(...) from error` | New type with explicit cause |
| Hide automatic context deliberately | `raise AppError(...) from None` | New type without displaying prior context |

questions.question: When should Python code raise TypeError or ValueError?
questions.title: TypeError vs ValueError in Python
questions.direct_answer: Raise `TypeError` when an argument has an unsupported type, and `ValueError` when its type is accepted but the supplied value is outside the valid domain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether Python's standard argument-error conventions are understood.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using one generic exception for every invalid argument or relying on assertions.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Treat the type as a stable category and the message as the specific violated rule.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `TypeError` means the kind of object is unsupported.
`ValueError` means the kind is accepted but the value is invalid.
Match the convention used by Python's own APIs when possible.
Include the parameter and violated rule in the message.
Do not use `assert` to validate public input.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`TypeError` and `ValueError` describe two different argument-contract failures. `TypeError` is appropriate when the function does not support the kind of object supplied. `ValueError` is appropriate when that kind of object is allowed but its particular value is outside the permitted range or format.

For example, a `set_timeout(seconds)` function may accept integers and floats. Passing a list is a type error because lists are not durations. Passing `-3` is a value error because a number is the right kind of input, but a negative timeout violates the rule. A useful message names the parameter and the expected contract.

This distinction lets callers handle mistakes precisely and matches familiar built-in behaviour such as `len(3)` raising `TypeError` and `int("three")` raising `ValueError`. Assertions are not a substitute for public input checks because optimized Python execution can remove assert statements. Use explicit validation and raise the documented exception. The short rule is: wrong kind means `TypeError`; right kind with an unacceptable value means `ValueError`.

sections.title: Treat the exception as part of the function signature
sections.content:
A signature says which arguments a function accepts; runtime validation completes that contract when annotations alone cannot enforce it. Choosing the conventional exception makes the API predictable to users, test code, and frameworks.

Be careful with Python's type relationships. Because `bool` is a subclass of `int`, an API that accepts counts may still need to reject `True` explicitly even though `isinstance(True, int)` is true. That is a value or policy decision the function should document.

Validation should occur near the public boundary. Internal helper code can then rely on the established invariant instead of repeatedly checking the same input. Messages support people, while the exception class provides the stable machine-readable category.

sections.title: Classify the broken argument contract
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Receive argument] --> B{Supported type?}
  B -->|No| T[Raise TypeError]
  B -->|Yes| C{Value satisfies rule?}
  C -->|No| V[Raise ValueError]
  C -->|Yes| R[Continue]
```
